title: Midterm Practice (do this last)
blurb: Midterm practice set. Use this after the earlier week tests.

questions.prompt: Which of the following bone types is the femur classified as?
questions.suggestedRationale: The femur is a long bone.

questions.prompt: What type of bone cell is responsible for bone resorption?
questions.suggestedRationale: Osteoclasts resorb bone; osteoblasts form bone.

questions.prompt: What is the function of synovial fluid?
options: To lubricate and reduce friction in joints
questions.suggestedLabel: C. To lubricate and reduce friction in joints
questions.suggestedRationale: Synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction.

questions.prompt: A greenstick fracture is best described as:
options: Partial break with one side bent
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Partial break with one side bent
questions.suggestedRationale: A greenstick fracture is an incomplete break with one side of the bone bent, common in children.

questions.prompt: What type of muscular dystrophy is most common in children?
questions.suggestedRationale: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common type in children.

questions.prompt: Osteoporosis results in:
questions.suggestedRationale: In osteoporosis, bone resorption exceeds bone formation, so mass and density fall.

questions.prompt: What is the primary cause of gout?
questions.suggestedRationale: Gout is caused by uric acid crystal deposits in joints.

questions.prompt: Which joint is most commonly affected by osteoarthritis?
questions.suggestedRationale: Osteoarthritis most often affects weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips.

questions.prompt: What are the significant early signs of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm?
options: severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
questions.suggestedLabel: B. severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia
questions.suggestedRationale: A ruptured cerebral aneurysm often presents with a sudden severe headache, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia.

questions.prompt: Typical signs of a TIA include:
options: transient muscle weakness in a hand or leg
questions.suggestedLabel: C. transient muscle weakness in a hand or leg
questions.suggestedRationale: A TIA causes brief, reversible deficits such as transient weakness in a hand or leg; consciousness is usually preserved.

questions.prompt: Which type of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) has the poorest prognosis?
questions.suggestedRationale: Hemorrhagic strokes generally have the poorest prognosis of the CVA types listed.

questions.prompt: Following a head injury, what is the most likely cause of secondary damage to the brain?
options: tearing of blood vessels as the brain rotates across the inside of the skull
questions.suggestedRationale: After the primary injury, secondary brain damage commonly comes from hematoma, infection, ischemia, or swelling.

questions.prompt: Collateral circulation is most likely to be present when a CVA results from:
questions.suggestedRationale: Collateral circulation is more likely when a CVA develops gradually from atherosclerosis than from a sudden embolus or rupture.

questions.prompt: Secondary brain tumors usually arise from:
questions.suggestedLabel: B. metastasized breast or lung tumors
questions.suggestedRationale: Secondary (metastatic) brain tumors most often come from lung or breast cancer.

questions.prompt: What does a vegetative state refer to?
options: Depression of the reticular activating system (RAS) and inability to initiate action
loss of awareness and intellectual function but continued brainstem function
continuing intellectual function but inability to communicate or move
disorientation and confusion with decreased responsiveness
questions.suggestedLabel: B. loss of awareness and intellectual function but continued brainstem function
questions.suggestedRationale: A vegetative state is loss of awareness and higher function with continued brainstem function.

questions.prompt: Loss of blood flow to the heart muscle that creates pain is called:
questions.suggestedRationale: Pain from inadequate blood flow to the heart is ischemic (anginal) pain.

questions.prompt: Pain that originates from damaged peripheral nerves is referred to as:
questions.suggestedRationale: Pain from damaged peripheral nerves is neuropathic pain.

questions.prompt: Abnormal changes in blood flow and metabolism in the brain may result in which type of headaches?
questions.suggestedRationale: Migraines are associated with abnormal cerebral blood flow and neurovascular/metabolic changes.

questions.prompt: Tension headaches are the result of:
questions.suggestedRationale: Tension headaches are commonly related to muscle tension from emotional stress.

questions.prompt: Myelinated A Delta fibers transmit which type of impulses?
questions.suggestedRationale: Myelinated A-delta fibers transmit sharp, acute pain; unmyelinated C fibers carry dull, chronic pain.

questions.prompt: Physical symptoms or Signs of pain that can be documented are:
options: Decreased heart rate and decreased blood pressure.
Elevated heart rate and elevated blood pressure.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Elevated heart rate and elevated blood pressure.
questions.suggestedRationale: Documentable physiologic signs of acute pain include an elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the function of endorphins in relation to pain?
options: Endorphins activate the SNS system for fight or flight
Transmit pain impulse through the spinal cord
Relay pain to the cerebral cortex
questions.suggestedRationale: Endorphins are endogenous opioids that block or reduce pain transmission.

questions.prompt: A reflexive stimuli results in which action?
options: Repeated flexion and extension of limbs
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Involuntary movement away from pain
questions.suggestedRationale: A withdrawal reflex produces involuntary movement away from a painful stimulus.

questions.prompt: The awareness of the brain for pain impulse that comes through is controlled by?
questions.suggestedRationale: The reticular activating system helps determine awareness of incoming sensory (including pain) impulses.

questions.prompt: Somatic Pain refers to pain that arises from?
questions.suggestedRationale: Somatic pain arises from skin, bone, or muscle; visceral pain arises from organs.

questions.prompt: Rust Colored sputum in patients with pneumonia is an indication of?
questions.suggestedRationale: Rust-colored sputum is a classic clue to pneumococcal (Streptococcus pneumoniae) pneumonia.

questions.prompt: An Epidural hematoma is located between?
questions.suggestedRationale: An epidural hematoma is between the dura mater and the skull.

questions.prompt: What does Gross level mean?
questions.suggestedRationale: “Gross level” refers to organs or organ systems, as opposed to the cellular/microscopic level.

questions.prompt: Which gram-positive bacillus causes flu-like symptoms and often causes bacterial infections of the skin or gastrointestinal (GI) tract of humans and cattle?
questions.suggestedRationale: Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a gram-positive bacillus that can infect skin or the GI tract in humans and cattle.

questions.prompt: What is an example of non-specific defense mechanism?
questions.suggestedRationale: Inflammation is a nonspecific defense; antigen–antibody responses, humoral immunity, and T cells are specific.

questions.prompt: Placing a client in which position reduces the force of gravity and affects many body functions?
questions.suggestedRationale: The supine position reduces the effect of gravity on many body functions (an important issue in immobility).

questions.prompt: Acute necrotizing fasciitis is a condition caused by infection with
questions.suggestedRationale: Acute necrotizing fasciitis is typically caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus.

questions.prompt: Which stress hormone is produced by Adrenal Cortex?
questions.suggestedRationale: Cortisol, the main glucocorticoid stress hormone, is made by the adrenal cortex (aldosterone is also cortical but is not the primary “stress hormone”).

questions.prompt: Difference between sensory nerve impulse and motor nerve impulse is that?
options: Sensory nerve impulse travels via Afferent Fibers
Motor Nerves control and use the Afferent Fibers
Sensory nerve uses spinal tract while Moto nerve connect directly to the cerebral cortex
They both use Afferent Fibers and Efferent Fibers
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Sensory nerve impulse travels via Afferent Fibers
questions.suggestedRationale: Sensory (afferent) fibers carry impulses toward the CNS; motor (efferent) fibers carry them away.

questions.prompt: Drugs that are designed to inhibit or slow down growth of microbes but not necessarily kill them are considered?
questions.suggestedRationale: Bacteriostatic agents inhibit microbial growth without necessarily killing the organisms.

questions.prompt: What is the term that is used when discussing the maximal amount of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs?
questions.suggestedRationale: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs.

questions.prompt: Depression is a common complication of which disorder?
questions.suggestedRationale: Depression is a common psychosocial complication of prolonged immobility.

questions.prompt: Secondary infections are common with AIDS. Which fungus is a common cause of death?
questions.suggestedRationale: Pneumocystis pneumonia (a fungal infection) is a classic, often life-threatening opportunistic infection in AIDS.

questions.prompt: What type of hypersensitivity is associated with incompatible blood transfusion?
questions.suggestedRationale: An incompatible blood transfusion is a type II (cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.prompt: The manifestations of a disease are best defined as the:
options: subjective feelings of discomfort during a chronic illness.
signs and symptoms of a disease.
factors that precipitate an acute episode of a chronic illness.
early indicators of the prodromal stage of infection.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. signs and symptoms of a disease.
questions.suggestedRationale: Manifestations of a disease are its signs and symptoms.

questions.prompt: Which of the following confirms the presence of active (reinfection) tuberculosis?
options: A positive skin test for TB
A calcified tubercle shown on a chest X-ray
Identification of acid-fast bacilli in a sputum sample
A history of exposure to individuals being treated for TB
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Identification of acid-fast bacilli in a sputum sample
questions.suggestedRationale: Active tuberculosis is confirmed by identifying acid-fast bacilli (or equivalent microbiologic evidence) in sputum; a skin test only shows exposure.

questions.prompt: When does flail chest usually occur?
options: An open puncture wound involves the pleural membranes.
The visceral pleura is torn by a fractured rib.
Several ribs are fractured at two sites.
Increasing fluid in the pleural cavity causes atelectasis.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Several ribs are fractured at two sites.
questions.suggestedRationale: Flail chest occurs when several ribs are fractured in two places, creating a free-floating segment.

questions.prompt: All of the following are examples of Advance Parkinson's Disease, Except?
questions.suggestedRationale: Loss of vision is not a typical feature of advanced Parkinson disease; swallowing difficulty, urinary problems, and orthostatic hypotension can occur.

questions.prompt: A disease which involves muscles and nerves and leads to tetany, esp in the face and hands is called?
questions.suggestedRationale: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular irritability and can cause tetany, including in the face and hands.

questions.prompt: One severe complication of a fracture of the pelvis or long bones like the femur which often occurs during transportation after injury is?
questions.suggestedRationale: Fractures of the pelvis or long bones (such as the femur) can release fat emboli, especially with movement after injury.

questions.prompt: A theory of pain control includes nerve synapses in the spinal cord and brain which permit pain to pass to the brain. This is called?
options: The Cerebral Cortex along with the Midbrain
Gate Theory or Gate Control System
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Gate Theory or Gate Control System
questions.suggestedRationale: Gate-control theory describes synapses in the spinal cord and brain that can permit or block pain signals.

questions.prompt: Healing of a would can be accomplished in several ways. A compound fracture which requires a longer healing time due to a large break and more inflammation than a simple fracture which would heal by which means?
questions.suggestedRationale: The wording points to how a simpler, cleaner wound or fracture heals: by first (primary) intention. A compound wound with more tissue damage is closer to second intention.

questions.prompt: Elephantiasis, caused by the obstruction of lymphatic vessels by parasitic worms, is an example of the condition known as:
questions.suggestedRationale: Elephantiasis from lymphatic obstruction by parasites is a form of lymphedema.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are common early signs of multiple sclerosis?
options: Paralysis of the lower body, impaired cognitive function
Areas of numbness, weakness in the legs, visual problems
Sensory deficit in the legs and trunk, memory loss, urinary incontinence
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Areas of numbness, weakness in the legs, visual problems
questions.suggestedRationale: Early multiple sclerosis often causes patchy numbness, leg weakness, and visual problems.
